extracted.intended_audience: The people of the State of New York; American citizens and voters considering the proposed Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: Argumentative analysis defending the proposed U.S. Constitution by setting out standards and principles for the allocation of powers between the federal government and the States (necessary-and-proper, supremacy, prohibitions on state actions, remedies for usurpation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on States issuing bills of credit and paper currency
rubrics_metrics.description: The extension of the prohibition to bills of credit; the power to make anything but gold and silver a tender in payment of debts is withdrawn from the States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: Paper money has produced pestilent effects on confidence between individuals and in public councils, harmed industry and morals, and injured the character of republican government. Allowing States to emit paper money or make non-gold/silver legal tender would multiply different currencies, impede intercourse among States, enable retrospective alterations in value that injure citizens of other States, and discredit the Union. Local mints under general authority could serve purposes of small-scale coinage without the mischiefs of state-regulated paper currency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of bills of attainder, ex post facto laws, and laws impairing contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: Bills of attainder, ex-post-facto laws, and laws impairing the obligation of contracts are contrary to first principles and are prohibited; the Convention added this constitutional bulwark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: These measures violate the social compact and sound legislation, threaten personal security and private rights, encourage speculations and jobs by influential actors, and produce repeated legislative interference. The prohibition serves as an additional fence to guard against arbitrary interference with personal rights and contracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on States imposing imposts or duties on imports/exports without Congress consent
rubrics_metrics.description: No State shall, without the consent of the Congress, lay any imposts or duties on imports or exports, except what may be absolutely necessary for executing its inspection laws; the net produce of such duties shall be for the use of the treasury of the United States; all such laws shall be subject to revision and control of Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: Regulation of trade must be submitted to federal councils to avoid conflicting state policies; the qualification secures reasonable discretion to States for convenience while giving the United States a check against abuse. Practical effect: prevents multiplicity of state trade duties that would impede interstate and foreign commerce; Congress retains supervisory authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on States laying duties on tonnage
rubrics_metrics.description: No State shall, without the consent of Congress, lay any duty on tonnage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context: Part of a package of constraints on State powers related to commerce and maritime obligations designed to preserve uniformity and prevent conflict with national interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on States keeping troops or ships of war in time of peace
rubrics_metrics.description: No State shall, without the consent of Congress, keep troops or ships of war in time of peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: Prevents independent State military establishments that could embroil the Union, preserve national uniformity in defense posture, and reduce risk of internal conflict among States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on States entering into agreements/compacts with other States or foreign powers
rubrics_metrics.description: No State shall, without the consent of Congress, enter into any agreement or compact with another State, or with a foreign power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: Prevents States from making treaties or compacts that could conflict with national foreign policy or produce inter-state disputes; preserves a single national voice in external relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on States engaging in war except when invaded or in imminent danger
rubrics_metrics.description: No State shall, without the consent of Congress, engage in war unless actually invaded, or in such imminent danger as will not admit of delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: Limits States' ability to commence hostilities, thereby protecting the Union from unilateral State acts of war and preserving national security management at the federal level, with narrow emergency exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary and Proper Clause (implied means to execute granted powers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress has the power 'to make all laws which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into execution the foregoing powers, and all other powers vested by this Constitution' — i.e., where the end is required, the means are authorized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: Without the substance of this power the Constitution would be a dead letter. The clause avoids the impracticality of attempting exhaustive positive or negative enumerations of all means. It authorizes implication and construction: particular powers necessary to effect general powers are included. Remedies for misconstruction of this clause are political and judicial (executive and judiciary expounding acts) and ultimately electoral (the people can annul usurpation by electing different representatives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supremacy of the Constitution, federal laws, and treaties
rubrics_metrics.description: This Constitution and the laws of the United States made in pursuance thereof, and all treaties made under the authority of the United States, shall be the supreme law of the land, and judges in every State shall be bound thereby, anything in the constitution or laws of any State to the contrary notwithstanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: Without supremacy, state constitutions could nullify national laws, creating incoherence (a law valid in some States but not others) and inverting the fundamental principles of government. Supremacy is essential to give effect to national powers and maintain uniformity across States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath or affirmation to support the Constitution by federal and State officers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senators and Representatives, and the members of the several State legislatures, and all executive and judicial officers, both of the United States and the several States, shall be bound by oath or affirmation to support this Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: State officers must be bound because they have essential agency in giving effect to the federal Constitution (e.g., in elections and administration). The distinction noted is that federal officers have no role in carrying State constitutions into effect, but State officers play a central role in implementing the federal system; requiring the oath secures their fidelity to the national charter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation principle: federal powers few and defined; State powers numerous and indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: The powers delegated by the proposed Constitution to the federal government are few and defined. Those which are to remain in the State governments are numerous and indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: Federal authority will principally address external objects (war, peace, negotiation, foreign commerce, treaties, finance); State governments will handle internal matters concerning lives, liberties, properties, and local order — suggesting the States retain broad practical influence and everyday governance responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical advantage of State governments in influence and resistance to federal encroachment
rubrics_metrics.description: State governments will have advantage over the federal government in immediate dependence, personal influence, numbers of officers, local familiarity, and capacity to resist or frustrate federal measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence and mechanisms: State officers and numerous local positions create stronger personal ties to the people; state execution of unpopular federal measures (or resistance) would quickly inflame local sentiment and create effective obstructions; states can coordinate resistance and appeal to popular power. Thus the design of the Constitution plus political realities reduce the risk that the federal government will overwhelm the States.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Constitution chiefly invigorates original federal powers rather than granting unnecessary new ones
rubrics_metrics.description: If the new Constitution be examined, the change proposed consists much less in the addition of new powers to the Union than in the invigoration of its original powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Powers relating to war, peace, armies, treaties, and finance already existed under the Confederation; the proposed change substitutes more effectual modes of administering them. The regulation of commerce is a notable addition but one generally accepted and not feared.
